title: Rotational Dynamics (tau_net = I_rot * alpha), Gear Ratios (N) and Reflected Inertia

blocks.x: Calculate the **moment of inertia** ($I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$) and **angular acceleration** ($\alpha = \tau_{\text{net}} / I_{\text{rot}}$) of a rotating link, and size a **gear ratio** ($N$) in Python by trading speed division ($\omega_{\text{out}} = \omega_{\text{in}} / N$) for torque multiplication ($\tau_{\text{out}} = \eta N \tau_{\text{in}}$) and $1/N^2$ **reflected inertia**.

blocks.x: Idea 1: Rotational Newton's Second Law ($\tau_{\text{net}} = I_{\text{rot}} \cdot \alpha$) and moment of inertia ($I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$)

items.x: **Primary resource:** [HyperPhysics — Moment of Inertia](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/mi.html) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`
**What to read:** Read exact headings **`Rotational-Linear Parallels`** and **`Moment of Inertia`**.
**What to skip:** Skip continuous volume integral derivations.

**Key takeaway:** Just as linear force accelerates a mass ($F_{\text{net}} = m \cdot a$), net rotational torque accelerates a spinning body according to **Rotational Newton's Second Law** $\tau_{\text{net}} = I_{\text{rot}} \cdot \alpha$, where $\alpha$ is **angular acceleration** (in **`rad/s^2`**) and $I_{\text{rot}}$ is the **moment of inertia** (rotational sluggishness, in **`kg·m^2`**). For a point mass $m$ at radius $r$ from the pivot, $I_{\text{rot}} = m \cdot r^2$. Notice the $r^2$: moving a heavy motor or gripper twice as far from the shoulder pivot makes its rotational inertia **$4\times$ larger**!

**Alternative resource:** [PhET — Torque](https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/torque) `[verify in-app]` — Open the **`Moment of Inertia`** tab `[verify in-app]` and watch how moving mass outward increases $I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$ and slows down angular acceleration $\alpha$.

blocks.x: Idea 2: Gear reduction ratio ($N$): torque multiplication, speed division, and $N^2$ reflected inertia

items.x: **Primary resource:** [Wikipedia — Gear train ("Gear ratio" & "Mechanical advantage")](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gear_train) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`
**What to read:** Read exact headings **`Gear train`**, **`Gear ratio`**, and **`Mechanical advantage`**.
**What to skip:** Skip epicyclic planetary carrier velocity tables (covered in Pass 2).

**Key takeaway:** Small DC motors spin very fast ($3{,}000\text{–}10{,}000\text{ RPM}$) with very little torque ($\sim 0.02\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$), whereas a robot arm needs slow, smooth speed and high torque. A **gearbox** with **gear ratio** $N = \frac{N_{\text{out}}}{N_{\text{in}}}$ (for example, $N = 50:1$) trades speed for torque by conserving mechanical power ($P = \tau \cdot \omega$ from `Lesson 00.1`):
**Speed divides by $N$:** $\omega_{\text{out}} = \frac{\omega_{\text{motor}}}{N}$
**Torque multiplies by $\eta \cdot N$:** $\tau_{\text{out}} = \eta \cdot N \cdot \tau_{\text{motor}}$ (where $\eta \approx 0.85$ is gearbox efficiency)

**Reflected inertia scales by $N^2$:** Because the motor shaft spins $N$ times faster than the load AND has $N$ times the leverage, the load inertia felt by the motor is divided by $N^2$ ($I_{\text{reflected}} = \frac{I_{\text{load}}}{N^2}$), or equivalently the motor's rotor inertia felt at the output joint is multiplied by $N^2$ ($I_{\text{joint}} = N^2 \cdot I_{\text{rotor}}$).
**Backlash:** Real gear teeth need a tiny gap so they don't jam; when the motor reverses direction, that free play (typically $0.5^\circ\text{–}2^\circ$ on hobby gearboxes) is called **backlash**.

blocks.x: By **Rotational Newton's Second Law**, the net torque $\tau_{\text{net}}$ (`N·m`) acting on a joint equals its **moment of inertia** $I_{\text{rot}} = m \cdot r^2$ (`kg·m^2`) multiplied by its **angular acceleration** $\alpha$ (`rad/s^2`). When a small, fast motor drives a heavy robot arm through a gearbox with **gear reduction ratio** $N = N_{\text{out}} / N_{\text{in}}$, speed division, torque multiplication, and reflected inertia follow five fundamental equations in base SI units:

Why does **reflected inertia** scale with **$N^2$** instead of $N$?
Use kinetic energy conservation (`Lesson 00.1`)! A load with inertia $I_{\text{load}}$ spinning at $\omega_{\text{out}} = \frac{\omega_{\text{motor}}}{N}$ carries rotational kinetic energy:

items.x: Load kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2} I_{\text{load}} \omega_{\text{out}}^2 = \frac{1}{2} I_{\text{load}} \left(\frac{\omega_{\text{motor}}}{N}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{I_{\text{load}}}{N^2}\right) \omega_{\text{motor}}^2$.

Thus, viewed from the fast-spinning motor shaft, the heavy arm feels **$N^2$ times lighter** ($I_{\text{load}} / N^2$)! Conversely, viewed from the outside world trying to push the robot arm by hand (backdriving the joint), the tiny motor rotor feels **$N^2$ times heavier** ($N^2 I_{\text{rotor}}$). With a $50:1$ gearbox, $N^2 = 2{,}500$!

**In Python 3:** Complete `point_mass_inertia_and_accel` (`TODO 1`) to compute $I_{\text{rot}} = m \cdot r^2$ (`kg·m^2`) and $\alpha = \tau_{\text{net}} / I_{\text{rot}}$ (`rad/s^2`), and complete `gearmotor_output` (`TODO 2`) to compute output torque $\tau_{\text{out}} = \eta N \tau_{\text{motor}}$, output speed $\omega_{\text{out}} = \omega_{\text{motor}} / N$, and reflected load inertia $I_{\text{load}} / N^2$ for a $50:1$ gearmotor.
**What is real-hardware only:** Physical gear-tooth **backlash** deadband (wiggling the output shaft slightly by hand while the motor rotor is held stationary).

def gearmotor_output(tau_motor_nm, omega_motor_rads, i_load_kgm2, gear_ratio_n, eff=0.85):
    tau_out_nm = eff * gear_ratio_n * tau_motor_nm
    omega_out = omega_motor_rads / gear_ratio_n
    i_refl_motor = i_load_kgm2 / (gear_ratio_n ** 2)
    return tau_out_nm, omega_out, i_refl_motor

def point_mass_inertia_and_accel(mass_kg, radius_m, net_torque_nm):
    i_rot = mass_kg * (radius_m ** 2)
    alpha_rads2 = net_torque_nm / i_rot
    return i_rot, alpha_rads2


def gearmotor_output(tau_motor_nm, omega_motor_rads, i_load_kgm2, gear_ratio_n, eff=0.85):
    tau_out_nm = eff * gear_ratio_n * tau_motor_nm
    omega_out = omega_motor_rads / gear_ratio_n
    i_refl_motor = i_load_kgm2 / (gear_ratio_n ** 2)
    return tau_out_nm, omega_out, i_refl_motor


i_load, alpha = point_mass_inertia_and_accel(mass_kg=0.50, radius_m=0.40, net_torque_nm=2.00)
t_out, w_out, i_refl = gearmotor_output(0.05, 300.0, i_load, gear_ratio_n=50.0, eff=0.85)

print(f"Load inertia I_rot = {i_load:.3f} kg*m^2 | Angular accel alpha = {alpha:.1f} rad/s^2")
print(f"50:1 Gearbox -> tau_out = {t_out:.3f} N*m | omega_out = {w_out:.1f} rad/s")
print(f"Reflected load inertia at motor shaft (I_load / N^2) = {i_refl:.6f} kg*m^2")

items.x: **Forgetting to square the radius $r$ in $I_{\text{rot}} = m \cdot r^2$ or the gear ratio $N$ in reflected inertia:** Lever torque scales with $r^1$ (`Lesson P.12`), but rotational inertia scales with **$r^2$**, and reflected inertia through a gearbox scales with **$N^2$**.

**Mounting a heavy elbow motor at the moving elbow joint instead of near the shoulder base:** Because $I_{\text{rot}} = m \cdot r^2$, putting a $0.3\text{ kg}$ motor out at the elbow ($r = 0.25\text{ m}$) burdens the shoulder with huge rotational inertia; mounting that motor near the shoulder ($r \approx 0$) and driving the elbow through a lightweight transmission (`Lesson 02.5`) slashes arm inertia!

**Why mount heavy motors near the base?** If you move a $0.4\text{ kg}$ wrist motor from $r = 0.40\text{ m}$ inward to $r = 0.10\text{ m}$ (4 times closer to the shoulder pivot), by what factor does its moment of inertia $I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$ around the shoulder decrease?

blocks.x: Because $I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$ depends on the **square** of $r$, reducing $r$ by $4\times$ reduces its moment of inertia by $4^2 = \mathbf{16\times}$!

items.x: **Speed and torque through a $10:1$ reduction:** A motor spins at $\omega_{\text{motor}} = 200\text{ rad/s}$ with torque $\tau_{\text{motor}} = 0.10\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ into an ideal ($\eta = 1.0$) $N = 10:1$ gearbox. What are $\omega_{\text{out}}$ and $\tau_{\text{out}}$?
Output speed: $\omega_{\text{out}} = \frac{200}{10} = \mathbf{20.0\text{ rad/s}}$.
Output torque: $\tau_{\text{out}} = 10 \times 0.10 = \mathbf{1.00\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}}$.

**Rotational Newton's Second Law** is $\tau_{\text{net}} = I_{\text{rot}} \cdot \alpha$, where **moment of inertia** $I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$ (`kg·m^2`) grows with the square of distance from the pivot.
A **gear ratio** $N = N_{\text{out}} / N_{\text{in}}$ divides speed by $N$, multiplies torque by $\eta N$, and scales **reflected inertia** by $N^2$ ($I_{\text{reflected}} = I_{\text{load}} / N^2$).
